interactions.summary: Students propose that Sinon's guilt, Virgil's denial, and Virgil's role as guide might explain the imbalance of punishment, while Jiang keeps returning to the unresolved paradox and says Purgatory will have to answer it.

claims.claim: A student distinguishes Sinon from Virgil by arguing that Sinon seems to know he lied, while Virgil has already forgiven himself for stealing from Homer.
Jiang questions whether Sinon thinks he did anything wrong at all, which keeps the moral accounting unstable rather than resolved.
Jiang says Virgil's anger does not prove confession but refusal: he is enraged because he does not want to admit the charge of plagiarism.
Jiang tells the class to keep asking why Virgil is not punished for his crimes and why hell is structured this way, treating the imbalance as a deliberate interpretive problem.

A student suggests Virgil's punishment may be indirect: the Aeneid implanted duty and coercive force into later readers, so Virgil's sentence is to escort souls through the consequences of his own poem.
Jiang corrects the student by saying Virgil is not literally the master of hell but a guide appointed by Beatrice who nevertheless knows hell intimately, which leaves the paradox intact.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang turns the whole Inferno reading into one burning question: why is the suspected poetic criminal unpunished while hell confidently punishes everyone else?
signature_moments.source_phrase: why is hell structured the way it is
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the architecture of hell itself part of the interpretive indictment rather than a neutral background.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil is not declared lord of hell, yet he still knows it well enough to climb Lucifer like he knows the place by heart.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he knows hell like the back of his hand
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's sense that proximity and competence can be as suspicious as formal authority.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture explicitly defers resolution of the Virgil/hell paradox to the Purgatory cantos, making the transition out of Inferno an interpretive continuation rather than a topic change.
